:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
First, we integrate with respect to $r,$ treating $\theta$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}{[{r}^{2}]}_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}{sin}^{2}⁡2\theta \,\text{d}\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Next, we recall the double-angle formula

$$
\cos{2x} = 1-2\sin^2 x.
$$

Substituting $x=2\theta$ and rearranging, we get

$$
\sin^22\theta = \dfrac12\left(1-\cos4\theta\right).
$$

 

Finally, we can finish our integral by integrating with respect to $\theta,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}{sin}^{2}⁡2\theta \,\text{d}\theta  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}\frac{1}{2}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡4\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}1-\operatorname{cos}⁡4\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{[\theta -\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta ]}_{0}^{\pi /8} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[(\frac{\pi }{8}-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}))-(0-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(0))] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(\frac{\pi }{8}-\frac{1}{4}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(\frac{\pi }{8}-\frac{2}{8}) \\  & =\frac{1}{32}(\pi -2)\end{aligned}
$$

:topic/knowledge-points.:knowledge-point/title: Evaluating Repeated Integrals Expressed in Polar Coordinates

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
![](images/17/1782385c55493892be0308ede1e4fbe5308ea9440e21b70cc2da7d7f01fb8dcd.png)

The region $D$ is the quarter-circle shown above. What is $\displaystyle \iint\limits_D y \sqrt{x^2+y^2} \: \textrm{d}A$
expressed in polar coordinates?
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
\iint\limits_{D} f(x,y) \ \mathrm d A = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta) \:  r \ \mathrm d r \mathrm d \theta.
$$

First, notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $1$ centered at the origin. In polar coordinates $(r, \theta),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
\Delta = \Big\{ (r,\theta) \: : \: 0 \leq r \leq 1, \: 0 \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{\pi}{2} \Big\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}y\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\sqrt{(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \sqrt{{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

:topic/knowledge-points.:knowledge-point/title: Rewriting a Double Integral Over a Circle or Part-Circle Centered at the Origin

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Integrate the function $f(x, y) = 15xy^2$ over the portion of the disk of radius $2$ centered at the origin, where $x \geq 0,y \geq 0.$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
\iint\limits_{D} f(x,y) \ \mathrm d A = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta) \:  r \ \mathrm d r \mathrm d \theta.
$$

First, let's sketch our region $D\mathbin{:}$

![](images/05/051cfbbf3fd37f01ff7e4442fccdc5ec4ce506e3c452b68bfa2ed5ae6e5cf6b9.png)

In polar coordinates $(r, \theta),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
\Delta = \left\{ (r,\theta) \: : \: 0 \leq r \leq 2, \:0\leq \theta \leq  \dfrac{\pi}{2} \right\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}15x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}15r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot (r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{2}15{r}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta {\int }_{0}^{2}5{r}^{4}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,{[{r}^{5}]}_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta ({2}^{5}-0)\text{d}\theta  \\  & =32{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =32{[{sin}^{3}⁡\theta ]}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =32({sin}^{3}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-{sin}^{3}⁡(0)) \\  & =32(1-0) \\  & =32.\end{aligned}
$$
